AI’s potential climate benefits outweighed by role in boosting fossil fuels, study finds
article.full_text: AI-driven productivity gains enable more planet-heating pollution from fossil fuels than they avoid from renewables, a study has found. Researchers modelled the technical potential for AI to boost clean power generation along with projections for how it can help produce coal, oil and gas. Across 64 scenarios, they found net yearly carbon pollution rose by 0.47-1.8 gigatonnes, or about 1-5% of the energy sector’s annual emissions. The study is the first to quantify the climate impact of AI across the full power sector. Previous research has explored its indirect climate benefits – such as reducing renewable downtime and optimising electricity grids – while ignoring the extra pollution from increasing productivity in drilling oil wells and extracting gas. “What most studies have done so far … is compare the datacentre energy use with the emissions savings AI has,” said Lynn Kaack, an assistant professor of computer science and public policy at the Hertie School who provided feedback on a draft of the research. “They completely omit this picture of AI causing increases in emissions.” The researchers found net emissions only fell in scenarios where AI did not increase productivity in the fossil fuel sector. If clean and dirty energy facilities were to adopt AI at similar rates, they found, the productivity gains for renewables would have to outpace those for fossil fuels by at least four times for emissions to break even. Holly Alpine, a co-author of the study and a former Microsoft employee who left to co-found the Enabled Emissions campaign group, said the research team used a conservative assumption that AI adoption would happen at the same rate for fossil fuels and renewables. “Fossil fuel applications are already happening at scale today – real contracts, real deployment, with evidence from industry operators and financial analysts,” she said. “Renewables applications are still largely at the pilot or academic-study stage – more speculative, more dependent on deployment barriers like permitting and interconnection getting resolved.” The International Energy Agency estimates that AI could boost technically recoverable oil and gas reserves by 5% and cut the cost of deepwater offshore projects by 10%. Oil and gas executives have been enthusiastic about the extra fuel that AI has allowed them to find, and celebrated its emerging impact as “the next fracking boom”. Saudi Aramco said last year that it had embedded AI “in everything”, increasing productivity and the number of wells, while earlier this summer Equinor attributed 27 discoveries on the Norwegian continental shelf to new seismic technologies and AI. The findings include the Lofn and Langermann oil wells, which the company said was the largest discovery it operated in 2025. “AI was key, from automated data interpretation to efficient well planning,” it said in a video at its capital markets day in June. Rystad Energy, an independent research and energy intelligence company based in Oslo, estimated in May that digitalisation and AI would create close to $500bn (£370bn) in cumulative value for fossil fuel exploration and production companies between 2026 and 2030 – the result of more efficient operations, increased production, and shorter development timelines. “The returns are already visible in the industry,” its analysts wrote, citing hundreds of millions of dollars in reported AI-related savings from Equinor and Abu Dhabi’s Adnoc. Climate scientists and energy experts have been troubled by the rapid construction of increasingly large and energy-hungry AI datacentres, which are typically powered by burning fossil gas. The researchers did not factor datacentre energy demand into their calculations but found AI enables productivity gains in the fossil fuel sector that result in emissions at least three times current estimates for datacentres. article.title: Oil prices hover near $90 a barrel and gold hits two-month high as Trump makes new demands on Iran – as it happened
article.full_text: Time to wrap up for the day. Our main stories: Thanks for reading! we’ll be back tomorrow. Bye! – JK My colleagues, the Guardian’s energy correspondent Jillian Ambrose and environment editor Damian Carrington are currently answering questions from readers about oil companies. Last week, they published a piece which revealed that biggest oil firms made $93bn in profits in three months amid the war in Iran and the climate crisis. They’re online now to discuss their story and any other questions you might have. Wall Street has got off to a lacklustre start. The S&P 500 if flat, Dow Jones managed a 0.4% rise and the Nasdaq is down 0.2%. Over here, the UK’s FTSE 100 eked out a 0.2% gain, up 24 points at 10,885. The Daw in Frankfurt is 0.4% ahead while the CAC in Paris edged 0.15% higher, the FTSE MIB rose 0.3% and the Ibex in Madrid climbed 0.5%. There is little economic data this week, apart from the US consumer price inflation reading for July, out on Wednesday and eagerly awaited by markets, followed by producer prices on Thursday. It is August… Oil prices have fallen back, after jumping more than 2% to the highest since late July earlier, with Brent touching $90.03 a barrel. Brent is now down 73 cents, or 0.8%, at $8.99 a barrel. Spot gold dipped 0.1% to $4,383 an ounce, affter hitting its highest level since 5 June at $4,434.84. Hotel prices have surged in key European cities as hundreds of thousands of tourists flock to see the first total eclipse visible from the continent this century. Iceland’s capital, Reykjavík, has seen one of the biggest jumps in hotel room prices, being one of the few accessible locations to see the full eclipse before evening on Wednesday. Tourists there have been shelling out $793 (£587) on average to secure a room on Wednesday, a 98% jump compared with the same day last year, according to data from the travel and hospitality data group Lighthouse Intelligence. Spain is also steeling itself for an influx of tourists, as one of the best places on the European continent to view the total solar eclipse. The finance ministry said on Monday that it expected 460,000 overseas tourists to visit specifically to see the eclipse. The rate for a room in A Coruña in the north of Spain was up 135% compared with last year to $451 on average, while prices in Mallorca, where the eclipse is expected to be visible on the horizon at sunset, were up by 24% at about $448. In Santiago de Compostela and Bilbao, hotel room prices have risen 34% and 67% respectively. Asda is to outsource its 3,500 cleaning staff in a move the GMB union has described as ‘detestable’. The workers will switch over to two third-party companies – Bidvest and NIC Cleaning Services – and retain their terms and conditions in the process. The shift comes as Asda battles to turn around slumping profits and falling sales since a debt-fuelled £6.8bn takeover in 2020 by the billionaire Issa brothers and the private equity firm TDR Capital. TDR has since taken majority control of the supermarket which is at risk of losing its spot as the UK’s third largest grocer to Aldi after non-fuel sales slid 3.3% to £21bn last year. The latest job changes come after Asda reduced its workforce by more than 7,000 roles last year. Hundreds of Asda security guards employed by outsourcing firm Mitie are being consulted on potential redundancy or reduced hours, more than 100 head office jobs have been recently cut while 1,000 jobs in its George clothing and homewares business were outsourced to logistics firm DHL last year. Rachelle Wilkins, GMB organiser, said: Loyal, hard working cleaning staff will be worried sick about whether their job will still pay the bills or whether the axe will fall on them.” She claimed that outsourcing companies often offered worse pay and conditions once they had taken over a service. Amnesty International says Farage putting ‘hate and inhumanity’ over leadership with El Salvador prison plan – as it happened
article.full_text: Andy Burnham has been warned that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so PC Andrew Harper’s killers are kept behind bars would force another spate of early releases before the next general election. A dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday. Amnesty International UK has condemned Reform UK’s proposal to send foreign prisoners to serve the rest of their sentences in El Salvador, saying it is an example of politicians choosing to put “hate, violence and inhumanity” ahead of leadership. (See 2.23pm.) GB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia. The Treasury “materially contributed” to the death of Chloe Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant who took her own life after facing disciplinary proceedings, a coroner has found. For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog. Danny Shaw, the home affairs commentator and former BBC correspondent who briefly worked as a Labour adviser on home affairs policy, says he thinks Downing Street is wrong to say it can’t find a way of excluding PC Andrew Harper’s killers from the early release scheme. (See 12.46pm.) This is wrong. Govt can block Pc Harper’s killers’ early release and ensure there’s enough prison space - through emergency legislation in September: 1. Exclude prisoners jailed for 10+ years for manslaughter from early release (220 people, including Pc Harper’s killers, Bowers and Cole) 2. Release on tag & curfew, after risk assessment, people jailed for up to 12 months (up to 2,700 people). All it takes is imagination and political will. Reform UK has confirmed that it would legislate to stop charities helping asylum seekers who come to the UK. Responding to an Express report about how many items Care4Calais has given to help migrants in France and the UK, Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, said: Care4Calais is not a charity. It is a facilitator of illegal migration, actively aiding the mass arrival of unvetted, fighting-age males into Britain at a cost of billions to the taxpayer. Successive Tory and Labour governments have colluded by looking the other way. Reform UK will pass the ‘Polanski Law’ to criminalise any act that assists or encourages illegal entry, punishable by two years’ imprisonment. We will treat those who enable this invasion as the accomplices they are and shut them down immediately. Yusuf described this as “Polanski’s law” when he first proposed it earlier this year because Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, is a proud supporter of the rights of asylum seekers. The Scottish Conservatives are urging the Scottish Greens to withdraw the whip from Q Manivannan MSP over their comment about rape being a “spectrum”. (See 1.48pm.) Meghan Gallacher, equalities spokesperson for the Scottish Tories, said: These remarks from an extremist Scottish Greens MSP were appalling and beyond the pale. It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences. Q Manivannan’s comments were so unacceptable that I believe Scottish Greens co-leaders Ross Greer and Gillian Mackay must now remove the whip from them. Aileen O’Connor, chair of the Thames Valley Police Federation, has said that Downing Street’s failure to block the early release of two of the men who killed PC Andrew Harper (see 12.46pm) is “indefensible”. In a statement, she said: The public are speaking loudly and clearly. They agree with us that the government are firmly on the wrong side of this. What they are doing is indefensible.
